claim:
Definition

For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared.

(a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are

$$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$

$$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$

with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless,

$$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$

because $\sum_{i=1}^3(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise, and summing the three integrable functions $3y_i^2\rho-|y|^2\rho$ and applying finite linearity of the integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) evaluates the sum as the integral of the pointwise-zero function; replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

(b) [General locally integrable branch] If instead $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is real and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)<\infty$ for a given integer $l\ge0$, then the degree-$l$ Cartesian moments of the same formula are absolutely convergent and defined; if the absolute weighted moment $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^L|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)$ is finite for some real $L\ge0$, then every integer Cartesian degree $0\le l\le L$ is defined, and in particular $Q=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$ is absolutely convergent, so that $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is a conclusion of this branch and not an added hypothesis. Here $\rho$ is restricted to the closed unit ball, where it is integrable by local integrability, and outside it $|y|^l\le|y|^L$; splitting the nonnegative integral over these two measurable sets and applying monotonicity and additivity of the integral gives $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le\int_{\overline B_1(0)}|\rho|+\int_{\{|y|>1\}}|y|^L|\rho|<\infty$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-metric-ball]]). The convention $|y|^0=1$ includes the origin, no compact support and no $L^1$-membership is assumed in this branch, and Cartesian monomials of degree $l$ have modulus at most $|y|^l$, so all lower moments, including $Q$, exist together with the degree-$l$ moment.

(c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e); for $N=0$ the lists are empty and every sum below is the empty sum $0$. Define

$$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l}\ (l\ge1),\qquad M^{(0)}:=Q,$$

$$Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$

finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again

$$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$

by finite distributivity. The points need not be distinct; charges at a common point add in every sum.

(d) [Reference point and scope] Every moment of (a)-(c) is computed about the chart origin of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; this origin is part of the definition. These are source moments of a prescribed static distribution, not momenta, rest masses, intrinsic spins, self-energies or dynamical quantities, and no field, force, equation of motion, equilibrium or empirical claim is made here; the static regime in which the source is read is the adopted idealisation of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (f). Every Cartesian degree $l$ in this definition is a nonnegative integer (the number of Cartesian indices); only the absolute weighted exponent $L$ in (b) may be any nonnegative real number.

surface_related_text: (e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

[F3] The weak solution predicate of the singular-source formulation is: for locally integrable $E,B$ and a source pair with volume part $(\rho_v,J_v)$ and singular part of point or stationary-sheet type, $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations when the four distributional pairings $\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$ vanish for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$; point sources with $C^1$ trajectory $z$ proper into $U$ have $\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle=q\int\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle=q\int z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ ([[def-em-weak-sources]](b),(e)).

[F6] Locally integrable functions are identified with their regular distributions, $\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$, and test functions are smooth with compact support in $U$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
claim:
Definition

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement
$$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$
pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$.

(d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps.

(e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

(f) [Conventions and scope] The regime is imposed in the one inertial frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; no claim is made that time independence survives a change of inertial description, and where a frame change is used the transformed fields must be rechecked. The static regime is an adopted idealization, not a dynamical stability theorem: static charged matter requires external support or an adopted equilibrium model. No equation is asserted here for singular sources beyond the dictionary of (e), and no empirical claim is made.

claim:
Definition

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and define $\nabla_t f=(\partial_1f,\partial_2f,0)$, $\Delta_t f=\partial_1^2f+\partial_2^2f$ and $\operatorname{div}_tu_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ for the stated regularity, using [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ where $A$ is either a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) or the explicit rectangular cross-section; the rectangle has corners and is treated by its open faces, not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. The separate smooth-cavity spectral branch uses an explicitly declared bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with its smooth PEC boundary; it is not the rectangular reflection class. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $n\cdot D=\sigma_f$ and $n\times H=K_f$ are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; for smooth fields the parities give $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb C$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal propagation constant; when $\beta$ is real, $\beta>0$ describes propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention, while a complex $\beta$ gives the spatial factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}\beta x_3}$ and may grow in the opposite direction; each consuming branch states its selection.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, Rectangular TE/TM candidates and the rectangular reflection class, declared smooth bounded PEC cavity spectral classes, and smooth straight-guide TEM potential branches (including the coaxial annulus) are within this geometry. No general non-rectangular TE/TM guide theory, circular-guide spectral classification, open-end or junction scattering, or arbitrary lossy model is supplied. The same stationary PEC geometry also hosts the explicitly declared constant scalar Ohmic cavity class and the full longitudinal finite-energy reflection class of the straight rectangular guide; constitutive and evolution claims belong to their consuming theorems, not this definition.

**Conventions fixed by this definition.** The definition records objects and conditions only: the guide and cavity regions, their open walls and outward normals, the ideal PEC boundary conditions with their interface reading and excluded idealization, the zero-normal-$B$ reflection class with its distributional divergence constraints, the axis-relative TE/TM/TEM terminology, and the separated phasor encoding of real fields. It asserts no field equation, no constitutive relation, no existence, uniqueness or completeness of modes, and no dissipation or energy claim; those belong to the consuming theorems, each of which restates the branch of the material model it uses. The rectangular cross-section is treated through its four open faces and is not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, and no pointwise condition on box edges is made.

claim:
Definition

Let $\omega>0$, $k:=\omega/c$ with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\mu_0>0$ the vacuum permeability of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and $p_0\in\mathbb C^3$ (the complex dipole-moment amplitude, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m$). Define, on the punctured space $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and all times $t\in\mathbb R$,

$$E_{\rm d}(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(-\frac{\mu_0\omega^2}{4\pi r}\,n\times(n\times p_0)\,e^{i(kr-\omega t)}\Bigr),\qquad B_{\rm d}(x,t):=\frac1c\,n\times E_{\rm d}(x,t),$$

where $r:=|x|$ and $n:=x/r$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), with the real part and complex exponential of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and [[def-complex-exponential]] and the componentwise real-part encoding convention of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] (the spatial amplitude here varies with $x$; no plane-wave instance is asserted). Call $(E_{\rm d},B_{\rm d})$ the **ideal harmonic electric-dipole radiation model of frequency $\omega$ and amplitude $p_0$**, and call $S_{\rm d}:=E_{\rm d}\times B_{\rm d}/\mu_0$ its model flux ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]); the model fields are read as an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]].

### Adopted status

This is an explicitly adopted ideal radiation-law model, fixed by the following declarations.

1. It is the leading transverse far-zone field of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]](c) evaluated at the harmonic transverse moment $V(u)=\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, i.e. at $p''$ for the waveform $p(u)=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u})$: by part (a) of [[lem-em-harmonic-forcing-periodic-response]] the second derivative of that explicit $C^\infty$ waveform is $\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, and substituting $u=t-r/c$ into $\mu_0\,n\times(n\times V(u))/(4\pi r)$ gives exactly $E_{\rm d}$, because $e^{i(kr-\omega t)}=e^{-i\omega(t-r/c)}$.
2. The model contains no independent magnetic-dipole or higher-multipole radiation, no near-zone or static field and no other radiating component.
3. It is not asserted to solve the vacuum Maxwell equations at finite $r$, to be the field of any actual source, to satisfy any boundary condition or to have finite total energy on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$.
4. For compact smooth conserved sources, comparison with these prescribed model fields uses the actual source's moment $p_{\rm act}(u)$ of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]], the harmonic waveform $p_{\rm h}(u)=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, their second-derivative mismatch

$$M(u):=|p_{\rm act}''(u)-p_{\rm h}''(u)|,$$

and the explicit $D,\Gamma$ bounds of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] (b), (c) and (e). A bound depending only on that source's $D$ and $\Gamma$ is valid when $M\equiv0$ on the observation window, in which case the theorem's leading fields for the source's moment coincide with the model fields; for $M\not\equiv0$ the comparison carries the additional mismatch term. The source's moment is not automatically the independently prescribed $p_0$. These actual-source comparisons assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) carried by the cited theorem. The explicit ideal fields themselves and their pointwise flux definition remain choice-free.

No measured, empirical or material-response content is adopted: $p_0$ is prescribed model data, not a derived polarizability.

### Well-definedness and conventions

**(a) [Compact smooth currents].** Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. The **magnetic dipole moment** of $J$ is the vector
$$m:=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of unit A m$^2$. The integral is computed componentwise over any nondegenerate closed bounding rectangle $Q$ containing $\operatorname{supp}J$, using the continuous functions $y\mapsto(y\times J(y))_i$ on $Q$ and their zero extension outside $Q$. For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields.

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

all vanish, all derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular
distributions of the fields and the source pairings being those of (b) and (c).

four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point
and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here;
adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after
this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining
this predicate.

occur only through their distributional derivatives paired with a test
function, and the source densities $\sigma,K$ occur only inside the ordinary
surface and time integrals of (b) and (c); products such as $\rho_sE$ or
$J_s\times B$ are not defined by this item. The definition asserts no existence
theorem for fields with singular sources, no conservation law (continuity for
these sources is proved separately where used) and no regularisation. Sources
that are not locally integrable and are not point or stationary-sheet sources,
moving sheets, line currents, and arbitrary products of distributions are
outside the definition.

Assume Countable Choice, inherited from the cited theorems. Work in the

constants $c,\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$
([[def-em-si-conventions]]), and the component dictionary of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]: $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F^{0i}=E_i/c$,
$F^{10}=-E_1/c$.

(a) [Source-free zero field] For $j\equiv0$ and $A=0$ the first-variation
coefficient (whose integral is multiplied by $c^{-1}$)
$-\mu_0^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu h_\nu+j^\nu h_\nu$ of clause (a) of
[[lem-em-compact-field-variation]] vanishes identically for every
$h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^4)$, because $F(A)=0$ and $j=0$; hence every
compact first variation of $S$ at $A=0$ is zero and $A=0$ is stationary.

(b) [A non-trivial compact test variation] Let $A$ be the smooth potential with
$A_0(x)=x^1$ and $A_1=A_2=A_3=0$, and let $j\equiv0$. Then
$F_{01}=-\partial_1A_0=-1$, $F^{01}=+1$, $F^{10}=-1$ and all other components
vanish, so the represented field is $E=(c,0,0)$, $B=0$ (clause (b) of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]) and $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=0$ on $U$. By
the equivalence of [[pthm-em-action-maxwell-variation]], $A$ is stationary;
directly, for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^4)$ the first variation of $S$
at $A$ is

$$\frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}S[A+sh]=-\frac{1}{c\mu_0}\int_U\bigl(\partial_0h_1-\partial_1h_0\bigr)d\lambda=\frac{1}{c\mu_0}\int_U\bigl(\partial_1h_0-\partial_0h_1\bigr)d\lambda=0,$$

where each of $\int_U\partial_0h_1\,d\lambda$ and $\int_U\partial_1h_0\,d\lambda$
vanishes by the fundamental theorem in one variable combined with Fubini, and
no boundary term appears because $h$ is compactly supported in $U$
([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]],
[[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

smooth prescribed source $j^0=c\rho(x^0)$, $j^i=0$, with nonzero nonnegative

$0\le\zeta\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$ with $\zeta=1$ near $[-1/2,1/2]$, and nonzero
nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty((-1,1)^3)$, supplied by
[[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]. Put

contravariant gauge variations

[[pthm-em-action-gauge-source-compatibility]]. Then, for every smooth potential
$A$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline U$,

$$S[A+\partial^\sharp\chi_\pm]-S[A]=\Bigl(\int_{-1}^1\rho\varphi_\pm'\,dx^0\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_{(-1,1)^3}\psi\,d^3x\Bigr)=\pm\Bigl(\int\rho\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\psi\Bigr),$$

$+j^\mu A_\mu$ coupling, the raised-vector/covariant-lowered gauge shift and
the conservation condition, using explicitly overlapping supports. If instead

every compact gauge difference is zero. No compact nonzero globally increasing
or decreasing function is used.

finite-region model; it asserts no existence of sources or fields, no numerical

Here the plane distribution is defined locally by $\langle\delta_S,\psi\rangle=\int\psi(x,y,0,t)\,dx\,dy\,dt$ for compactly supported tests on the laboratory region; no global compactness of this plane is asserted. These are the local planar counterparts of the compact-interface hypotheses in [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]. Write $E_{j\,t}$, $E_{j\,n}$ for the tangential and normal parts of the one-sided trace $E_j$ and $D_j$ ($j=1$ on $\Omega_-$, $j=2$ on $\Omega_+$), defined by the Euclidean decomposition against $n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

**(a) [Tangential field]** $n\times[E]=0$, i.e. $E_{2t}=E_{1t}$: the tangential electric field is continuous across the interface.

**(b) [Normal displacement]** $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$, i.e. $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}-\varepsilon_1E_{1n}=\sigma_f$, hence $E_{2n}=\frac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2}E_{1n}+\frac{\sigma_f}{\varepsilon_2}$.

**(c) [No free sheet charge]** If $\sigma_f=0$, then $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}=\varepsilon_1E_{1n}$ and $E_{2n}=\frac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2}E_{1n}$: the normal component is scaled by the positive ratio $\varepsilon_1/\varepsilon_2$, so $E_{2n}$ and $E_{1n}$ have the same sign (and vanish together). Precisely, $E_{2n}=E_{1n}$ if and only if $(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}=0$: equality holds when the normal field is zero even for unequal permittivities; if $E_{1n}\ne0$, it holds exactly when $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$. A free surface charge $\sigma_f\ne0$ modifies the normal condition as displayed and is not silently set to zero.

**(d) [Magnetic companions]** $n\cdot[B]=0$ and, with $K_f=0$, $n\times[H]=0$; for nonmagnetic media with $H=\mu_0^{-1}B$ on both sides this gives $B_{2n}=B_{1n}$ and $B_{2t}=B_{1t}$.

Example

Let the laboratory frame and units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], with spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, $z=x_3$, $r=|x|$ and the applied field along $e_3$. Fix $a>0$ with $\overline B_a\subseteq\Omega$, so that the interface $S=\{r=a\}$ below lies in the laboratory region, a field magnitude $E_0>0$ and constants $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\in(0,\infty)$ (the interior and exterior permittivities of the elementary branch of [[post-em-material-closure]], the material being at rest in the laboratory frame), and put

$$C:=\frac{3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}},\qquad d:=\frac{E_0a^3(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}})}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}}.$$

Consider the time-independent potentials

$$\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}(x):=-C\,E_0\,z\quad(r<a),\qquad \varphi_{\mathrm{out}}(x):=-E_0\,z+\frac{d\,z}{r^3}\quad(r>a),$$

with fields $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ and $D:=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}E$ inside, $D:=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}E$ outside ($E$ being of the class of [[def-em-fields]] restricted to this time-independent configuration). Write $S=\{r=a\}$ and $n=e_r$ for the outward normal. Then:

**(a) [Harmonicity]** $\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ on $r<a$ and $\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ on $r>a$ in the classical sense of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], and the potentials and their first derivatives extend continuously to the closed sides of $S$.

**(b) [Interface conditions]** With one-sided traces at $r=a$, $\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}\,\partial_r\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\,\partial_r\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$ on $S$; equivalently the tangential electric field and the normal component of $D$ are continuous. These electric matching identities hold independently of any magnetic completion. In addition, declare the static completion $B=H=0$, $\rho_f=J_f=0$, with any constant symmetric positive-definite permeability and the zero-conductivity branch $\sigma=0$, $J_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$ of [[post-em-material-closure]]. The four fields then satisfy all four thin-interface macroscopic equations distributionally with $\sigma_f=K_f=0$, and the joint one-sided regularity at the compact sphere verifies the hypotheses of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]. Assume its inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention ([[def-countable-choice]]) for this distribution/surface reading.

**(c) [Asymptotics]** $\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}(x)+E_0z=dz/r^3$ and $\nabla(\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}+E_0z)=O(r^{-3})$ as $r\to\infty$: the difference from the applied uniform potential decays like $r^{-2}$ and its gradient like $r^{-3}$.

**(d) [Uniqueness in the declared class]** Let $(\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{in}},\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{out}})$ be $C^2$ on the closed ball $\overline{B_a}$ respectively on every closed exterior region $\{a\le r\le R\}$, harmonic on $r<a$ and $r>a$, satisfying the same interface conditions (b), and satisfying $|\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}+E_0z|\le M/r$ for some $M$ and all sufficiently large $r$. Then $\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}=\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$. Hence the displayed pair is the unique solution of the dielectric-sphere transmission problem in that class, existence being exhibited explicitly; the uniqueness proof uses only the Green identity, the matching conditions and the decay, with no maximum principle.

**(e) [Fields, polarisation and induced dipole]** On $r<a$ the field is uniform, $E=C E_0e_3$ with $D=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}CE_0e_3$; outside, the field is that of the applied uniform field plus the field of a point dipole at the origin with moment $p=4\pi\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\,d\,e_3$; the interior polarisation is $P_{\mathrm{in}}=(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}-\varepsilon_0)CE_0e_3$ and the bound surface charge density on $S$ is $\sigma_b=n\cdot(P_{\mathrm{in}}-P_{\mathrm{out}})$, the singular coefficient of $\rho_b=-\operatorname{div}P$ at $S$ (with the exterior polarisation $P_{\mathrm{out}}=(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}-\varepsilon_0)E_{\mathrm{out}}$).

**(f) [Regime and scope]** The computation is a quasistatic result of the declared linear branch at $\sigma_f=0$; using $p$ as a dynamic wave polarisability of the sphere requires a separate quasistatic/dipole approximation and is not asserted here. The example asserts no material data and no empirical claim.

surface_related_text: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface and finite-source branches. Adopt the electric-dipole radiation-law idealization whose leading far fields and angular flux are the dipole expressions of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]], evaluated for the prescribed smooth waveform $p(u)=p_0\cos(\omega u)e_3$ with $\omega>0$ and $p_0\ne0$. This is an explicit ideal radiation-law model, not an eternal compact-time source claimed to satisfy that theorem with $D=0$. The waveform is a moment convention of [[def-em-electric-moments]], not measured data. All exact quantities below refer to that ideal leading radiation law. Then:

(b) [Angular power density] The retarded-time angular power density of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] is $$\frac{dP}{d\sigma}(n,u)=\frac{\mu_0|n\times p''(u)|^{2}}{16\pi^{2}c}=\frac{\mu_0\omega^{4}p_0^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega u)}{16\pi^{2}c}\,\sin^{2}\theta,$$ the $\sin^{2}\theta$ pattern with zeros along $\pm e_3$ and maximum in the equatorial plane; its integral over the sphere is $$\int_{S^2}\frac{dP}{d\sigma}d\sigma=\frac{\mu_0\omega^{4}p_0^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega u)}{6\pi c},$$ using $\int_{S^2}\sin^{2}\theta\,d\sigma=8\pi/3$ from [[lem-em-sphere-zonal-moments]](a).

(d) [Scope] The computation is the exact dipole law of the model; a finite prescribed source realizes it only within the absolute error bound of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] with its $D(u)$, and a physical antenna's feed, current distribution and material realization are additional source models not supplied here. The average in (c) is taken in the retarded-time variable, not in observation time; no measurement, radiation resistance, matching condition or effective area is reported, and no empirical claim is made.

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the dipole theorem [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] with its source class and constants; the waveform $p(u)=p_0\cos(\omega u)e_3$, $\omega>0$, $p_0\ne0$; the construction data $\eta,\sigma,p_\eta,\rho,J$ of clause (e).

[L1] Dipole theorem: for a source of the compact smooth conserved class, $p\in C^\infty$ with $p''(u)=\int J_t(y,u)dy$, $|V(n,u)-p''(u)|\le D(u)$ with $D(u)=\frac{a}{c}\int_{B_a}\sup_{|v-u|\le a/c}|J_{tt}(y,v)|dy$; the leading far fields are $E_{\mathrm{lead}}=\mu_0n\times(n\times V)/(4\pi r)$, with errors $\Gamma_E/r^{2}$ and $(\Gamma_B+\Gamma_E/c)/r^{2}$, and the angular power density limit is $\mu_0|n\times V|^{2}/(16\pi^{2}c)$ with total error $|R(u)|\le\mu_0(2|p''|D+D^{2})/(4\pi c)$. ([[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] (a)-(d))

[L6] Conventions: $e_3$ is a unit vector, the moment convention is that of [[def-em-electric-moments]], $\varepsilon_0\mu_0c^{2}=1$ and the dipole theorem's source class is the compact smooth conserved one whose retarded fields are constructed by [[pthm-em-retarded-potentials]]. ([[def-em-electric-moments]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[pthm-em-retarded-potentials]])
claim:
Example

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface and finite-source branches. Adopt the electric-dipole radiation-law idealization whose leading far fields and angular flux are the dipole expressions of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]], evaluated for the prescribed smooth waveform $p(u)=p_0\cos(\omega u)e_3$ with $\omega>0$ and $p_0\ne0$. This is an explicit ideal radiation-law model, not an eternal compact-time source claimed to satisfy that theorem with $D=0$. The waveform is a moment convention of [[def-em-electric-moments]], not measured data. All exact quantities below refer to that ideal leading radiation law. Then:

(a) [Fields] With $n=\sin\theta\cos\varphi\,e_1+\sin\theta\sin\varphi\,e_2+\cos\theta\,e_3$, $\theta\in[0,\pi]$, the leading far fields are $$E_{\mathrm{lead}}(rn,u+r/c)=-\frac{\mu_0\omega^{2}p_0\cos(\omega u)}{4\pi r}\,n\times(n\times e_3),\qquad B_{\mathrm{lead}}=\frac{n\times E_{\mathrm{lead}}}{c},$$ with $|n\times(n\times e_3)|=|\sin\theta|$, so the amplitude pattern is $\propto\sin\theta$ and vanishes on the dipole axis $\theta\in\{0,\pi\}$.

(b) [Angular power density] The retarded-time angular power density of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] is $$\frac{dP}{d\sigma}(n,u)=\frac{\mu_0|n\times p''(u)|^{2}}{16\pi^{2}c}=\frac{\mu_0\omega^{4}p_0^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega u)}{16\pi^{2}c}\,\sin^{2}\theta,$$ the $\sin^{2}\theta$ pattern with zeros along $\pm e_3$ and maximum in the equatorial plane; its integral over the sphere is $$\int_{S^2}\frac{dP}{d\sigma}d\sigma=\frac{\mu_0\omega^{4}p_0^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega u)}{6\pi c},$$ using $\int_{S^2}\sin^{2}\theta\,d\sigma=8\pi/3$ from [[lem-em-sphere-zonal-moments]](a).

(c) [Period average] The mean of the total power over one retarded-time period $u\in[0,2\pi/\omega]$ is $$\frac{\omega}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi/\omega}\frac{\mu_0\omega^{4}p_0^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega u)}{6\pi c}\,du=\frac{\mu_0\omega^{4}p_0^{2}}{12\pi c}.$$

(d) [Scope] The computation is the exact dipole law of the model; a finite prescribed source realizes it only within the absolute error bound of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] with its $D(u)$, and a physical antenna's feed, current distribution and material realization are additional source models not supplied here. The average in (c) is taken in the retarded-time variable, not in observation time; no measurement, radiation resistance, matching condition or effective area is reported, and no empirical claim is made.

(e) [Actual compact-window realization] Choose a compact smooth time cutoff $\eta\equiv1$ near one selected period, a nonnegative $C^\infty$ bump $\sigma$ supported in $B_a$ with integral $1$, and $p_\eta(u)=\eta(u)p_0\cos(\omega u)e_3$. Define $\rho(y,u)=-p_\eta(u)\cdot\nabla\sigma(y)$, $J(y,u)=p_\eta'(u)\sigma(y)$. These are smooth compact spacetime sources, satisfy continuity, carry zero total charge and have moment $p_\eta$. On the chosen period the moment equals the harmonic waveform, while the actual retarded field has the full $D(u)$, $\Gamma_E/r^{2}$ and $(\Gamma_B+\Gamma_E/c)/r^{2}$ errors of the dipole theorem. Its asymptotic total-power deviation from the ideal law is bounded by that theorem's explicit $R(u)$; its period-averaged deviation is bounded by the average of $|R(u)|$. The condition $V=p''$ is a sufficient ideal transverse-moment condition; it is not equivalent to $D=0$. No eternal nonzero harmonic moment is asserted for a compact-time source.

Example

Take the unit square $D=[0,1]^2$ as parameter region, an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, a function $a\in C^2(I)$ with $a>0$ everywhere, and

$$r(u,v,t):=\bigl(a(t)u,\ a(t)v,\ 0\bigr),\qquad B:=e_3,\qquad v(x,t):=\frac{a'(t)}{a(t)}\,(x_1,x_2,0).$$

Then $r$ is of class $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2\times I$, the tangent vectors are $r_u=(a,0,0)$ and $r_v=(0,a,0)$ with $r_u\times r_v=(0,0,a^2)\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I^\circ=D^\circ\times I$, the field $B$ is constant with $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and $v$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3\times I$ with $v(r(u,v,t),t)=(a'(t)u,a'(t)v,0)=r_t(u,v,t)$; so the data satisfy the standing hypotheses of [[def-em-moving-patch]]. For every $t\in I$ the parametrized flux is $\Phi(t)=a(t)^2$, hence $\Phi'(t)=2a(t)a'(t)$; the fixed-time surface integral of $\partial_tB$ is $0$; and $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=-2(a'(t)/a(t))\,e_3$, so patch Stokes gives $\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r=-2a(t)a'(t)$, exactly the sign in the formula of [[lem-em-moving-flux]]. Dropping the term $-\oint(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ — that is, treating the moving patch as fixed — would leave $\Phi'=0$, which the direct derivative contradicts whenever $a'(t)\ne0$. All maps are of the stated regularity and no singular support is involved; the example verifies the sign convention and the necessity of the motion term, and asserts no physical law.

Let the incidence angle be given by $\sin\theta_i=4/5$, which exceeds the critical angle $\theta_c$ with $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1=2/3$, so $|\kappa|=K_1\sin\theta_i=(6/5)(\omega/c)>(\omega/c)=K_2$. Then with $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^{2}-K_2^{2}}=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$ and $k_{13}=(\omega/c)(3/2)(3/5)=(9/10)(\omega/c)$: (i) [Reflection] $Y^{s}_1=9/(10\mu c)$, $Y^{s}_2=i\sqrt{11}/(5\mu c)$ and $$r_s=\frac{9/10-i\sqrt{11}/5}{9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5},\qquad |r_s|=1,\qquad t_s=\frac{9/5}{9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5},\qquad |t_s|^{2}=\frac{324}{125};$$ the reflection factor is the phase $r_s=e^{-2i\varphi}$ with $\varphi=\arctan\!\bigl(2\sqrt{11}/9\bigr)\approx0.63514703$ (about $36.39124^\circ$), i.e. the reflected wave acquires the phase $-2\varphi\approx-1.27029406$ (about $-72.78249^\circ$); (ii) [Transmitted field] the transmitted field is $E_t(x,t)=e^{-\beta x_3}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(E_t\hat y\,e^{i(|\kappa|x_1-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with $\beta=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$: it decays by the factor $e^{-\sqrt{11}/5}\approx0.51514$ when $x_3$ increases by $c/\omega$, its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically, $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle\equiv0$, while its tangential averaged flux is positive, $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}\,\frac{(6/5)(\omega/c)|E_t|^{2}}{2\mu\omega}=e^{-2\beta x_3}\frac{3|E_t|^{2}}{5\mu c}$; (iii) [Flux budget] $|r_s|^{2}+(\operatorname{Re}Y^{s}_2/Y^{s}_1)|t_s|^{2}=1+0=1$, so the whole incident normal averaged flux is reflected, while the evanescent field carries a tangential averaged flux only; (iv) [Scope] the example is an exact deterministic computation of the lossless interface model for declared parameters; it reports no measurement, and the presence of a tangential evanescent flux is not a claim about information speed or signal propagation.

claim:
Example

Assume the Countable Choice convention of [[pthm-em-image-method-certificate]] and [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] ([[def-countable-choice]]). In the ideal grounded-plane configuration of [[pthm-em-image-method-certificate]]: vacuum half-space $H=\{x_3>0\}$, point charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ at $p=ae_3$ ($a>0$), field $E_I$ given by the image potential, and $E_I$ has the Coulomb singularity $(q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0))(x-p)/|x-p|^3$ of the source charge as $x\to p$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d), [[def-em-fields]]). Split the field near $p$ as

$$E_I(x)=E_q(x)+E_{\rm ext}(x),\qquad E_q(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{x-p}{|x-p|^3}\quad(x\ne p),$$

the **self-field** $E_q$ of the source charge and the **external (mirror) field** $E_{\rm ext}:=E_I-E_q$, which is $C^\infty$ on a neighbourhood of $p$ (it is minus the gradient of the smooth mirror term $-q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)|x+ae_3|^{-1}$). Then:

(a) [External field at the charge] the external field at the location of the charge is

$$E_{\rm ext}(p)=-\frac{q}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}\,e_3 .$$

It is the gradient of the mirror term evaluated at $p$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Force on the held charge] under the adopted external Lorentz coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](i) at zero velocity, a test particle of charge $q$ held at $p$ experiences the electric force

$$F=q\,E_{\rm ext}(p)=-\frac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}\,e_3,$$

strictly attractive toward the plane when $q\ne0$ and zero when $q=0$, of magnitude $q^2/(16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2)$; the particle's own field is excluded from the coupling by the postulate, so the result is a two-body-style external force of the mirror field and is not a self-force.

(c) [Reading and scope] for either nonzero sign of $q$ the force is attractive (the magnitude depends on $q^2$), while $q=0$ gives zero force; the induced total plane charge is $-q$ and its distribution is concentrated under the charge; the example is the exact ideal-model result for a held point charge, an ideal grounded plane and the adopted static external force law. It asserts no measurement, no dynamics of the charge (no motion or radiation), no finite-plane or finite-conductor correction, no self-force and no claim that the pair of idealisations is realised by an apparatus; the source is the idealised stationary point charge of [[pthm-em-image-method-certificate]](e), not a declared compact-source model. Here the displayed force is the electric contribution at rest. Holding the charge at $p$ requires a balancing support force $F_{\rm support}=-F$; the held trajectory is not asserted to solve the equation with the electric Lorentz force as its sole force.

surface_related_text: (b) [Classical equations] $\operatorname{div}E=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ pointwise on $\Omega$; hence the fixed-time pair $(E,0)$ satisfies the reduced smooth-branch electrostatic equations with zero volume source on $\Omega$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (c), [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]);

(e) [Normalization] for fixed $r_0$, $\varphi(\rho)\to-\infty$ as $\rho\to\infty$ if $\lambda>0$ and $\to+\infty$ if $\lambda<0$, while changing $r_0$ to $r_0'$ shifts $\varphi$ by $\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\log(r_0'/r_0)$ and leaves $E$ unchanged. For $\lambda\ne0$ the infinity normalization of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (b) is therefore unavailable; for $\lambda=0$ the field, potential and line source are zero and all cutoff energies and fluxes vanish; and $\Omega$ is not star-shaped (for every $a\in\Omega$ the segment from $a$ to $-a$ passes through the axis, which is not in $\Omega$), so [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]] does not apply to $\Omega$, although the displayed $\varphi$ still satisfies $E=-\nabla\varphi$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]);

(g) [Scope and idealization] the line charge $\rho_\lambda$ is *not* a source type of [[def-em-weak-sources]]: only point sources and stationary sheets are declared there, and no line current, moving sheet or other distribution is included. The item therefore verifies classical, flux and distributional identities for an explicitly specified distribution $\rho_\lambda$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with a noncompact singularity; it is not a framework postulate covering infinite line charges, asserts no physical realisation, equilibrium or empirical content, and is not a compact-source Coulomb corollary. Real line-like distributions have finite length and transverse size, and their far fields and energies require their own hypotheses.

[F2] The logarithm is smooth on $(0,\infty)$ with derivative $1/t$; the divergence and curl are the classical operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and the regime conventions are those of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]).

Let $c>0$ and $a>0$, and define $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by $z(s):=(\sqrt{c^{2}s^{2}+a^{2}},0,0)$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]). Then:
(a) $z$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ and $|z'(s)|<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$; nevertheless there is no constant $v_*<c$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$, because $|z'(s)|\to c$ as $s\to\pm\infty$;
(b) at the event $(x,t)=(0,0)$ the retarded equation $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$ of [[def-em-retarded-point-geometry]] has no solution in $\mathbb R$: the equation reads $-s=\sqrt{c^{2}s^{2}+a^{2}}/c$, whose right-hand side is at least $a/c>0$, and squaring both sides would give $c^{2}s^{2}+a^{2}=c^{2}s^{2}$, i.e. $a^{2}=0$, contrary to $a>0$. Hence pointwise subluminality of a smooth curve does not by itself produce the retarded root, and the uniform bound $v_*<c$ of [[def-em-retarded-point-geometry]], or an explicit cone-intersection hypothesis, cannot be dropped; the supplier [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] indeed assumes such a uniform bound.
(c) [Scope] This is a mathematical example about the prescribed curve and the root equation. The curve is future timelike pointwise ($|z'(s)|<c$ for every $s$) but not uniformly subluminal; it is not asserted to be the worldline of any physical charge, and no measurement is reported. The example contradicts no theorem: it exhibits a curve lying outside the hypotheses of the root lemma.

[L4] The retarded equation and the uniform-bound hypothesis are those of [[def-em-retarded-point-geometry]]; the cited root lemma states its existence and uniqueness result for curves with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for all $s$. ([[def-em-retarded-point-geometry]], [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]])

— an explicit switched-history distribution for $z(t)=0$ on $(0,\infty)$, with
no compensating current or source contribution at the appearance event; it does
not satisfy the proper-graph hypothesis of the zero-endpoint continuity branch
of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) — and let $J:=0$ be the zero distribution. Then:

(b) Consequently there are no locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $U$
satisfying the four weak residual identities of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e)
with the source pair $(\rho,0)$, the $\rho$-pairing being the explicit pairing
displayed above and $J=0$: such fields would satisfy the distributional
continuity identity of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](b), which applies to
every distributional source pair for which the four identities hold, and (a)
contradicts it. The source pair $(\rho,0)$ is therefore incompatible with the
formal four residual identities themselves; it is not one of the declared
point sources of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b), because the properness hypothesis
fails here as recorded, and no fields turn it into an admitted singular-source
model under [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]].

construction: by the endpoint clause of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],
the same trajectory on a bounded interval $I_0=(a,b)$ has
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$
with $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$. A switched point charge with $J=0$ and no endpoint
or current term is thus inadmissible; a switched charge must be accompanied by

not satisfy the proper-graph hypothesis of the zero-endpoint continuity branch
of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) — and let $J:=0$ be the zero distribution. Then:

(a) $\partial_t\rho=q\,\delta_{(0,0)}$ and $\operatorname{div}J=0$
([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]), hence
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{(0,0)}\ne0$ in
$\mathcal D'(U)$: for every test function $\psi$,
$\langle\partial_t\rho,\psi\rangle=-q\int_0^\infty\partial_t\psi(0,t)\,dt=q\,\psi(0,0)$,
because $t\mapsto\psi(0,t)$ is smooth with compact support. In particular the
continuity identity fails at the appearance event $(0,0)$.

(b) Consequently there are no locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $U$
satisfying the four weak residual identities of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e)
with the source pair $(\rho,0)$, the $\rho$-pairing being the explicit pairing
displayed above and $J=0$: such fields would satisfy the distributional
continuity identity of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](b), which applies to
every distributional source pair for which the four identities hold, and (a)
contradicts it. The source pair $(\rho,0)$ is therefore incompatible with the
formal four residual identities themselves; it is not one of the declared
point sources of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b), because the properness hypothesis
fails here as recorded, and no fields turn it into an admitted singular-source
model under [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]].

(c) The failure is exactly the omitted endpoint term of the point-source
construction: by the endpoint clause of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],
the same trajectory on a bounded interval $I_0=(a,b)$ has
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$
with $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$. A switched point charge with $J=0$ and no endpoint
or current term is thus inadmissible; a switched charge must be accompanied by
an explicit current or endpoint source term, which the weak equations of
[[def-em-weak-sources]] then require to satisfy continuity.

This is a mathematical incompatibility statement about a declared source
model, not a report of a measurement: no apparatus, sampling model,
uncertainty or empirical claim is involved.

[F1] The model data and elementary regularity: $E$ is bounded, equal to $-(\sigma/\varepsilon_0)e_3$ on the open slab $\{|x_3|<h\}$ and to $0$ outside it, hence locally integrable; $\varphi$ is bounded, affine on the closed slab, constant on the two open half-spaces, and continuous on $\mathbb R^3$ with equal one-sided values on each plane: $\varphi|_{\Pi_+}=\sigma h/\varepsilon_0$, $\varphi|_{\Pi_-}=-\sigma h/\varepsilon_0$; on each of the three open regions $\{|x_3|<h\}$, $\{x_3>h\}$, $\{x_3<-h\}$ the maps are $C^\infty$ (affine or constant), and $E=-\nabla\varphi$ there by the classical gradient of affine functions; on the slab $|E|=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ and $E$ is normal to the planes, outside it $E=0$; the plane functionals $\delta_{\Pi_\pm}$ are finite-order distributions on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]]).

Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the integral and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). **Declare the ideal parallel-plate model** of two infinite parallel charged planes in vacuo, read as equipotential ideal conductor surfaces of the same equilibrium structure as [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] (the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with fields [[def-em-fields]]): for a separation parameter $d>0$, half-separation $h=d/2$, a surface-density parameter $\sigma>0$ (C m$^{-2}$) and the framework constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], the model consists of the field
$$E(x):=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}e_3,&|x_3|<h,\\[2pt]0,&|x_3|>h,\end{cases}\qquad x=(x_1,x_2,x_3),$$
together with the plane densities $+\sigma$ on $\Pi_+:=\{x_3=h\}$ and $-\sigma$ on $\Pi_-:=\{x_3=-h\}$, and with the piecewise potential $\varphi(x):=+\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}x_3$ for $|x_3|\le h$, $\varphi:=+\dfrac{\sigma h}{\varepsilon_0}$ for $x_3\ge h$ and $\varphi:=-\dfrac{\sigma h}{\varepsilon_0}$ for $x_3\le-h$. Then:
(a) [Direct distributional verification] $E$ and $\varphi$ are locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off $\Pi_+\cup\Pi_-$ with $E=-\nabla\varphi$ there, $\varphi$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$ and constant on each plane with the values $\varphi|_{\Pi_+}=+\sigma h/\varepsilon_0$, $\varphi|_{\Pi_-}=-\sigma h/\varepsilon_0$; and in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$
$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\bigl(\delta_{\Pi_+}-\delta_{\Pi_-}\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,$$
where $\delta_{\Pi_\pm}(\psi):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\psi(x_1,x_2,\pm h)\,dx_1\,dx_2$ for compactly supported smooth $\psi$ are the plane distributions defined by the iterated Lebesgue integrals. Equivalently, the model realises the static electrostatic equations with the declared pair of plane densities and no other source, and the potential differences read off $\varphi$ are $\varphi(h)-\varphi(-h)=2\sigma h/\varepsilon_0=\sigma d/\varepsilon_0$.
(b) [Uniform field and voltage] the field between the planes has constant magnitude $|E|=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ and is normal to the planes, and the potential difference between the plates is $V:=\varphi|_{\Pi_+}-\varphi|_{\Pi_-}=\sigma d/\varepsilon_0$.
(c) [Charge, capacitance and energy of the ideal model] for any Lebesgue-measurable region $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ with finite positive area $A=\lambda_2(P)>0$ the charge on the portion of area $A$ of the positive plate is $Q:=\sigma A$, so $Q=(\varepsilon_0A/d)V$ with the geometric ratio
$$C:=\frac QV=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}>0,$$
independent of $\sigma$ and $V$; and the field energy contained in the slab of area $A$ between the plates is
$$U=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\text{slab of area }A}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac{\sigma^2Ad}{2\varepsilon_0}=\frac12QV=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12CV^2 .$$
(d) [Relation to the bounded-conductor theorem and scope] the linearity $Q=CV$, the positivity $C>0$ and the energy identities $U=\frac12QV=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12CV^2$ are exactly the conclusions that [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] proves for bounded conductor configurations with prescribed potentials and a grounded reference; this example verifies them directly for the ideal model because the infinite planes and the unbounded declared field are outside that theorem's hypotheses (compact conductors in a bounded vacuum region) and outside the declared stationary-sheet source type of [[def-em-weak-sources]], exactly as the ideal line source lies outside the compact-source types of the electrostatic page. No approximation theorem from finite plates to the infinite model is asserted; for a finite real plate pair the uniform-field model neglects the fringing field near the edges, which is not computed here, and the idealisation also omits the finite-thickness, material, transient and measurement content of any real capacitor.

claim:
Example

Fix $K>0$, $\omega:=cK$, $k:=Ke_3$, $E_0>0$
(unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$), the amplitude $e:=E_0e_1$ and
$b:=k\times e/\omega=(E_0/c)e_2$, and let $(E,B)$ be the corresponding
plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with energy
density $u$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]; write
$\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$. Then:

(i) [Explicit density] $E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$,
$B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$ and
$u(x,t)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2\theta(x,t)$, a nonnegative function vanishing
exactly on the nodal planes $\cos\theta=0$; the period average at every fixed
$x$ is $\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2>0$, uniformly in $x$ and $t$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]](a)).

(ii) [Unbounded box integrals] Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and let
$R\ge(\omega|t|+\pi/4)/K$. On the sub-box
$Q_R:=[-R,R]^2\times[(\omega t-\pi/4)/K,\,(\omega t+\pi/4)/K]$ of the box
$[-R,R]^3$ one has $\cos^2\theta\ge1/2$, hence
$u\ge\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2$ there; both boxes are product boxes with finite
volume ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]), $u$ is continuous on
them and therefore Riemann integrable
([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]), and
monotonicity of the multidimensional Darboux integral
([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]) gives
$$\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,dx\;\ge\;\int_{Q_R}u(x,t)\,dx\;\ge\;\frac{\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{2}\,\mathrm{vol}(Q_R)\;=\;\frac{\pi\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{K}\,R^2\;\longrightarrow\;+\infty\quad(R\to\infty).$$
Consequently no finite value is attained by the box integrals as
$R\to\infty$: the ideal plane wave has infinite total energy in the
box-exhaustion sense, in contrast to the total energy of a single wave 'mode'
being finite on any bounded box.

(iii) [Contrast with compactly supported data] If instead the constrained data
of [[pthm-em-general-wave-ivp]] vanish off a compact set, then by clause (d) of
that theorem the fields have compact spatial support at each time, and the
instantaneous total energy is the integral of the continuous density $u$ over
a compact set, hence finite. So finite total energy is available for
compactly supported data, while the ideal plane wave of (i)-(ii) is not a
finite-energy configuration.

(iv) [Scope] The example is an exact computation for the ideal plane wave; it
reports no measurement, and "infinite total energy" means the divergence
statement (ii), not a claim about any laboratory field or finite beam.

In the RL branch of [[pthm-em-rl-lc-dynamics]] with the declared units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let the source voltage be the constant $V_0\in\mathbb R$, let $R>0$ and $L>0$, let $t_0\in J$ and $I_0\in\mathbb R$, with $J$ an interval and derivatives read in the model's domain-relative convention, through the stated $C^1$ open-neighbourhood extension for a non-open $J$. Then the unique $C^1$ solution of $L\dot I+RI=V_0$, $I(t_0)=I_0$, is
$$I(t)=\frac{V_0}{R}+\Bigl(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\Bigr)\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\Bigr),\qquad t\in J .$$
In particular $I(t)-V_0/R=(I_0-V_0/R)\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ and hence $|I(t)-V_0/R|=|I_0-V_0/R|\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ for every $t\in J$, with time constant $\tau=L/R$; $I\equiv V_0/R$ is the unique stationary solution; if $J$ is unbounded above, then $I(t)\to V_0/R$ as $t\to+\infty$ along $J$; and the transient part is the free decay $\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ of the initial deviation $I_0-V_0/R$. For $J=\{t_0\}$ the restriction is $I(t_0)=I_0$ and the jets are those of the same formula read through the stated extension, giving $\dot I(t_0)=(V_0-RI_0)/L$. The computation is conditional on the adopted lumped model, constant elements and fixed geometry; no measurement is involved.

[F1] In the RL branch let $L>0$, $R\ge0$ and let $V:J\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Then the initial value problem $L\dot I+RI=V$, $I(t_0)=I_0$, has exactly one $C^1$ solution on every nondegenerate interval $J$, namely $I(t)=\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)\left[I_0+L^{-1}\int_{t_0}^t\exp(R(s-t_0)/L)V(s)\,ds\right]$; for $J=\{t_0\}$ the restriction is $I(t_0)=I_0$ and the canonical extension for the constant source $V(t_0)$ has jet $\dot I(t_0)=(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$; the RL solution uses no choice principle. ([[pthm-em-rl-lc-dynamics]]).

(a) [Potential form] Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain and let $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb C)$ (with real-valued potentials included) satisfy $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$ (the plane Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]; a $C^2$ function with $\Delta\varphi=0$ is called harmonic). For either sign $\zeta\in\{+1,-1\}$ define $\tilde E:=-\nabla\varphi$, $\beta:=\zeta\omega/v$ and $\tilde H:=\zeta e_z\times\tilde E/Z$; then the separated real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(\tilde Ee^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(\tilde He^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)})$ satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations with $E_z=B_z=0$ (TEM), and the PEC condition on a smooth wall with unit normal $n$ is equivalent to $\partial_\tau\varphi=0$ along that boundary curve, so that $\varphi$ is constant on each connected component of $\partial A$. Moreover, if $A$ is star-shaped ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), every separated TEM phasor with $C^1$ transverse amplitudes has on the interior a complex harmonic potential $\varphi\in C^2(A;\mathbb C)$, obtained by applying [[cor-closed-exact-and-conservative-equivalence-on-star-shaped-domains]] to the real and imaginary electric amplitudes separately. If the field is nonzero, the equations force $\beta^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$, hence $\beta=\pm\omega/v$, and $\tilde H=\beta e_z\times\tilde E/(\omega\mu)$, giving the two displayed signs. If the field is zero, $\tilde E=\tilde H=0$ solves the equations for every longitudinal label $\beta$, with no dispersion conclusion. The boundary potential description requires the stated continuous differentiable boundary trace (in particular the initial $C^2(\overline A)$ potential has it); the interior exactness supplier alone is not asserted to produce a real potential or automatic boundary extension.
(b) [Single-conductor obstruction] If in the potential-form setting $\partial A$ is connected, then $\varphi$ is constant on $\partial A$, hence $\varphi$ is constant on $\overline A$ by the two-dimensional classical Dirichlet uniqueness [[cor-uniqueness-for-the-classical-dirichlet-problem]], applied to its real and imaginary parts with their respective constants as second solutions, and therefore $\tilde E=\tilde H=0$: a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the potential form. The same potential-form obstruction applies to a rectangular cross-section with a potential in $C^2(A)\cap C(\overline A)$ having constant boundary trace, because this uniqueness supplier does not require a $C^1$ boundary. For rectangular separated TEM amplitudes that are $C^1$ on the interior and continuous on the closure with the classical PEC traces on open edges, the star-centre radial primitive extends continuously to the rectangle closure. The edgewise tangential derivative is the electric trace, so PEC makes the potential constant on each open edge and continuity joins those constants at the corners. Thus this stated rectangular class has no nonzero TEM field.
(c) [Coaxial example] For the following Lebesgue polar-coordinate energy calculation assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). (d) [Scope] The obstruction clause (b) is proved for the continuous-boundary harmonic-potential form. The star-shaped interior classification in (a) covers both signs and the zero field, with boundary conclusions under the stated potential-trace hypotheses; the general reduction of an arbitrary TEM field to the potential form on a merely simply connected non-star-shaped cross-section is not asserted here. surface_related_text: Assume the lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $L=\begin{pmatrix}L_1&M\\M&L_2\end{pmatrix}$ be a constant symmetric block of its inductance matrix with $L_1,L_2>0$. Let $I_1,I_2:J\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ currents on an interval $J$ (each extending to a $C^1$ map on an open interval containing $J$, as in the model's conventions) with terminal voltages $V_\alpha=\sum_\beta L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\beta$. Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the realization and bounded-linking clauses (b), inherited from the linkage and energy suppliers.

(a) [Energy and instantaneous power] the stored inductive bookkeeping energy is
$$W(t)=\tfrac12L_1I_1(t)^2+\tfrac12L_2I_2(t)^2+MI_1(t)I_2(t),$$
and $V_1I_1+V_2I_2=\dot W$ by part (a) of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]]; the mutual term increases the energy for currents of the same sign and decreases it for opposite signs (as the sign of the product $I_1I_2$ indicates when $M>0$).

(b) [Perfect linkage and the bound] if the two currents are realised by fixed compact smooth conserved profiles of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b) with linkage matrix $L$ as in [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]], then $W(t)\ge0$ for all currents, and evaluating the quadratic form on both $(\sqrt{L_2},-\sqrt{L_1})$ and $(\sqrt{L_2},+\sqrt{L_1})$ gives the bound
$$|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2};$$
moreover if $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ with $s\in\{+1,-1\}$ (perfect linkage), the null direction $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-s\sqrt{L_1})$ has $J_I=0$ pointwise by the vanishing clause of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]](c).

[F1] The adopted lumped model carries the Faraday branch relation $V=L\dot I$: each terminal potential is the rate of change of the branch flux linkage $LI$; the matrix and terminal data are declared model data. ([[post-em-circuit-approximation]]).

[F2] For constant symmetric $L$ and a $C^1$ current $I$ with open-neighbourhood extension, $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V,I\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle$ with $V=L\dot I$, and for a smooth compact conserved-profile realization the quadratic form equals the frozen magnetic field energy $\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|B_{J(t)}|^2$ at each time. ([[pthm-em-inductor-energy]]).

[F3] For fixed compact smooth conserved profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$ with linkage matrix $L=(L_{\alpha\beta})$ one has $U(I)=\frac12\int\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|B_{J_I}|^2\ge0$, and $U(I)=0$ exactly when $J_I=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha=0$ pointwise; the matrix is positive definite exactly when the profiles are pointwise linearly independent. ([[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]).

[F4] The compact smooth current class consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. ([[def-em-steady-current-regime]]).

Writing $\Phi_c:=\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)$ for the common flux linkage, the terminal voltages are
$$V_1=N_1\dot\Phi_c,\qquad V_2=N_2\dot\Phi_c,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{V_1}{N_1}=\frac{V_2}{N_2}=\dot\Phi_c,$$
and the stored energy is $W=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$; equivalently the induced emfs $e_\alpha:=-V_\alpha$ satisfy $e_1/N_1=e_2/N_2=-\dot\Phi_c$. This is the explicitly adopted common-linkage ('ideal transformer') model with turns ratio $N_1:N_2$.

(d) [Limitations] for an imperfect realized linkage, $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, the perfect common-flux voltage ratio is not an identity for all current histories; a particular history can nevertheless satisfy that ratio accidentally (including both voltages zero). Reversing the second winding retains $s=-1$: with $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ put $\Phi_c=\Lambda(N_1I_1+sN_2I_2)$ and obtain $V_1/N_1=V_2/(sN_2)=\dot\Phi_c$, with the same energy $\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$. Winding resistance, hysteresis and core loss, stray capacitance, magnetising current and finite permeability are outside the declared model and are not inferred from it. No measurement is involved; the statements are conditional computations in the ideal model. Regularity on a non-open interval uses the stated $C^1$ neighbourhood extension; if the interval is a singleton its terminal-voltage jets are those of a specified extension, not derivatives inferred from its value restriction.

$$\rho(x):=\frac{3Q}{4\pi a^3}\,\mathbf 1_{\{|x|<a\}}(x),\qquad E(x):=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\begin{cases}x/a^3,&|x|<a,\\ x/|x|^3,&|x|\ge a,\end{cases}\qquad \varphi(x):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{Q(3a^2-|x|^2)}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a^3},&|x|\le a,\\ \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|},&|x|\ge a.\end{cases}$$
(The value of $\rho$ on the sphere $\{|x|=a\}$ is immaterial: it is a Lebesgue-null set by the polar calculation $\lambda_3(S_a)=4\pi\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{a\}}(r)r^2dr=0$, since the one-dimensional singleton has measure zero ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).) Then:

(a) [Regularity and gradient] $E$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$, of class $C^\infty$ on each of the open regions $\{|x|<a\}$, $\{|x|>a\}$; $\varphi\in C^1(\mathbb R^3)$, its displayed branch derivatives agree on $\{|x|=a\}$, and $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]);

$$\operatorname{div}E(x)=\rho(x)/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E(x)=0$$
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]);

(c) [Weak equations] the pair $(E,(\rho,0))$ satisfies the spatial distributional equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$: $E$ is $C^1$ on each side of the sphere $S_a=\{|x|=a\}$ with one-sided continuous traces that agree, $[E]=0$, so [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] gives
$$\operatorname{div}E=\{\operatorname{div}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[E]\,\delta_{S_a}=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[E]\,\delta_{S_a}=0,$$
with $\rho$ the displayed locally integrable density and no surface-charge term ([[def-em-weak-sources]], [[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]] for the sphere as a compact embedded smooth hypersurface); by the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e) these are the weak equations of the static model for this source, with zero singular part;

$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a},$$
computed with the polar formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]); the value agrees with the smooth-source identity of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] although the density here is only piecewise continuous;

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $d>0$ and $I_1,I_2\in\mathbb R$; let wire 1 be the declared ideal line current of amplitude $I_1$ along the third coordinate axis and wire 2 the translate of that ideal line current by $d\,e_1$, of amplitude $I_2$ ([[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c2)), and adopt for the force on wire 2 the thin-wire coupling (W) of [[pthm-em-magnetic-loop-force-torque]], restricted to the external field of wire 1. Then the force per unit length on wire 2 is
$$\mathbf f=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}\,e_3\times e_2=-\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}\,e_1,$$
i.e. attraction towards wire 1 (direction $-e_1$) for currents in the same direction ($I_1I_2>0$), repulsion for opposite directions, and magnitude $\mu_0|I_1I_2|/(2\pi d)$ per unit length. The comparison uses only the external field of wire 1 at the position of wire 2; the self-fields and the mechanical support forces of the two infinite wires are excluded, no claim is made about the total force on either infinite wire, and no measurement is involved.
